articles.title: Hegseth’s former chief of staff calls for his ouster
articles.summary: Joe Kasper said that the DOD head had “been belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him.”
articles.body:
The former top aide to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is calling on him to resign, saying he has badly mismanaged both the Pentagon and ongoing war in Iran, and let showmanship get in the way of doing his job well.

"Pete's ability to be effective has been constrained and very soon he'll have lost any ability to be effective," Joe Kasper, who was chief of staff to Hegseth for the first three months of the Trump administration, told POLITICO. "For that reason and others it's time for Pete to call it quits."

In a nearly hourlong interview, Kasper critiqued Hegseth's tenure as secretary, assailing his choice to fire top military leaders as well as senior Black and female military brass , his obsession with image and his handling of the Iran war, which he called a "shitshow." He also said there was no evidence that several Pentagon officials who were fired last year for allegedly leaking to the media ever shared material without authorization to reporters.

"Pete's been belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him or any memory of his service," Kasper said.

A senior Pentagon official, speaking on behalf of the Defense Department, said in a statement to POLITICO that it wasn't surprising that a "disgruntled former staffer—someone who could barely survive ninety days in the building—is now peddling made up gossip to the media."

"Secretary Hegseth is laser focused on restoring lethality to the force and supporting our warfighters, while Mr. Kasper is more focused on rewriting history to cover for his own failed tenure," the official said.

President Donald Trump said he was keeping Hegseth as the Pentagon's leader amid speculation by senior administration officials and other Republicans about Hegseth's standing in the administration. The party's losses in the midterms were attributed by some in part to the ongoing war in Iran. Hegseth's footing in the administration has also been helped by the elevation of his ally Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff.

Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) recently wrote in his memoir that his deciding vote to confirm Hegseth was the "biggest regret of my career," and even Trump ally Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) said several weeks ago that he had "no idea" what Hegseth's Iran strategy was.

While Hegseth survived a House impeachment vote earlier this month, he could face another attempt in the next Congress when Democrats assume control of both chambers.

By calling for his resignation, Kasper, an Air Force veteran, said he wanted to "speak truth to power" after a sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier admonished people around Hegseth to stop laughing during a ceremony on Veterans Day. The viral video led Hegseth to award the sentinel a Joint Service Commendation Medal.

Kasper said the award was an "attempt to trivialize" the moment, as "if that makes it all okay."

A former chief of staff to disgraced former Rep. Duncan D. Hunter (R-Calif.), Kasper said he first met Hegseth around 2010 when Hegseth headed up Concerned Veterans for America and Kasper was on Capitol Hill. Kasper would later work at the Department of Homeland Security, the Navy and the Air Force in the first Trump administration.

His critics said last year in a New York Magazine story that Kasper quickly ran into trouble in his new role at the Pentagon. The magazine said that he was often late to meetings and developed a reputation for not fully carrying out critical tasks. Kasper told the publication that some of the criticism was "arbitrary and subjective."

After departing the chief of staff role, Kasper was a special government employee at the Pentagon for a time, working on the Defense Department's advisory boards. Since leaving his full-time job at the department, he has been a principal at Ervin Graves Strategy Group, advising clients on defense issues, and is chair of the advisory board of the publicly-traded rare earths company REalloys.

During his stint at the Pentagon in 2025, Kasper was a leading figure in the firings of senior adviser Dan Caldwell, Hegseth deputy chief of staff Darin Selnick and Colin Carroll, chief of staff to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg. The trio were ousted in April 2025 amid a leak investigation. At the time, they denied disclosing sensitive information without authorization.

Kasper told POLITICO that he now believes there was no evidence that they had ever leaked anything, an assertion backed up by the New York Times , which reported that an internal investigation into leaks didn't find any wrongdoing on the part of the three men. Earlier this year, Caldwell rejoined the administration in the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

Kasper had requested an investigation into Defense Department leaks in March 2025, which related to the development of military plans to "reclaim" the Panama Canal, Elon Musk's visit to the Pentagon and a temporary pause in the collection of intelligence for Ukraine.

Kasper left his role as Hegseth's chief of staff soon after his colleagues were ousted. Hegseth said Kasper had not been fired and expressed support for him.

"Joe is a great guy, great American," Hegseth told Fox News at the time . "He has done a fantastic job for us at the Defense Department. … You make changes over time, and we're grateful for everything Joe's done."

In recounting his issues with Hegseth, Kasper also predicted that it would be impossible for the combative Hegseth to work with Congress or get proper funding for department priorities.

"He's not just burned bridges up on the Hill," he said. "He's napalmed them. … He's going to be suffocated, and it's not like it's going to be a slow suffocation. It's going to be a quick asphyxiation."

Kasper said that he realized within a week of starting at the Pentagon that Hegseth's focus was "all about Pete rather than the institution and the men and women who support it."

"There's quite an emphasis on the showmanship," he said. "The virtues of humility and basically service before self and those things have disappeared. I didn't see those at the start, and see them ever less so now."

Hegseth "overindulged in ego, in attitude, and in entitlement," he said.

Kasper called Hegseth's promotion of issues like measuring soldiers' testosterone "distractions," saying it was "silly" how an early emphasis on bringing back the warrior ethos and an increased prioritization of recruiting and retention standards had devolved into a measure of how many jumping jacks and push-ups a soldier could do.

Kasper also said that the Pentagon's senior leadership had been hollowed out by the removal or resignations of many top leaders, including Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, Army Chief of Staff Randy George, and Gen. Christopher T. Donahue, the top Army general in Europe . Driscoll left after months of tensions with Hegseth; the Pentagon didn't give official reasons for forcing George and Donahue to retire early.

"These are real inspirational figureheads who were committed to the mission, but publicly they were treated in ways that would have made you think otherwise," Kasper said, adding it was disrespectful to treat them poorly after many had dedicated their lives to serving the country.

He called the Army "essentially leaderless," adding: "At almost every high-profile position, or every senior leader position, there's a vacancy."

Kasper said that Hegseth would rank close to the bottom 10% of defense secretaries in American history.

"I think history will be much crueler to him than I could be," he said.

articles.title: House GOP races the clock as absences derail final agenda
articles.summary: House Republicans have just three weeks left in session to advance their legislative priorities before Democrats take control of Congress in January, leaving a narrow window to push through an assortment of unfinished business. At the top of the list is reaching an agreement on a stopgap measure, known as a continuing resolution (CR), or…
articles.body:
House Republicans have just three weeks left in session to advance their legislative priorities before Democrats take control of Congress in January, leaving a narrow window to push through an assortment of unfinished business.

At the top of the list is reaching an agreement on a stopgap measure, known as a continuing resolution (CR), or passing all 12 appropriations bills before the Dec. 11 funding deadline to avert a government shutdown. Republicans also face pressure to get the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), permitting reform legislation, a farm bill and other items across the finish line.

But it won’t be an easy task for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to wrangle his caucus, especially as he struggles to keep his own members in Washington long enough to get the work done.

Attendance problems have already begun disrupting the House floor schedule. GOP leaders postponed a procedural rule vote Wednesday over absences and canceled Friday’s votes altogether. Twenty-one Republicans missed votes on Thursday morning, following 14 absences the previous day.

Johnson will need near-unanimous support on any procedural rule if he decides to bring a bill to the floor via regular order, requiring most of his conference to be present as he juggles a razor-thin margin. The House this week took up bills under a fast-track process known as suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority for passage and is typically reserved for legislation with broad bipartisan support. Because those bills often attract significant Democratic backing, Republicans can afford absences without jeopardizing passage.

Johnson called the attendance issue “a great frustration” and told reporters he plans to address it directly with members. He went a step further on Friday and urged his colleagues to show up and vote in a letter posted to the social platform X.

“To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term,” he said.

House lawmakers left Washington for Thanksgiving recess, leaving them with a little more than a week to address government funding after they return. House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole (R-Okla.) told reporters that he wants to pass 12 appropriations bills and has little appetite for a CR.

The three appropriations bills the House has passed so far — funding military construction and the Department of Veterans Affairs, the State Department and agriculture and rural development — represent some of the lowest-hanging fruit. Johnson is sure to face much tougher resistance — both from Democrats and within his party — when the topic shifts to funding other agencies, including the departments of Homeland Security, Defense, and Health and Human Services.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine), meanwhile, released text for all 12 bills negotiated by the upper chamber this month. Republicans on the Senate Appropriations Committee previously told The Hill there are still lots of moving pieces but that the end result is likely going to be some kind of short-term CR.

Still, Cole said in a statement that he’s “used to long odds and tight timelines.”

“Neither has ever deterred me from doing the work. A lame duck doesn’t have to leave full-year bills dead in the water. … The biggest disservice to the American people would be not to try. I refuse to let any opportunity available pass us by simply because some are already looking at the next Congress while this one still has votes to take,” Cole said.

Rep. Nick LaLota (R-N.Y.), who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, told The Hill that “everything should be on the table to pass 12 appropriations bills.”

Also on the GOP to-do list is the annual defense policy bill, which is facing an uphill climb in the Senate over its $1.15 trillion request. Senate Democrats blocked the upper chamber’s version of the bill back in July, citing President Trump’s handling of the Iran war.

And any NDAA passed by the Senate must be reconciled with the House version, which passed the lower chamber in July.

The House is also looking to take up a major bipartisan permitting reform bill that passed the Senate this week. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) wrote on X that the legislation would “cut red tape, create jobs, and lower costs for families,” and he urged the House to “finish the job” by sending the bill to Trump’s desk.

The bill will likely pass the lower chamber, but the path to getting it across the finish line remains uncertain. Johnson could move it under regular order, where attendance issues could complicate passage of a rule. It’s unclear whether he has enough Democratic support to move it under suspension of the rules.

Trump has also been pushing Congress to pass legislation that would reauthorize spending for food and agricultural programs, writing in a Truth Social post this week that “IT IS TIME TO DO IT AGAIN, and FAST.”

“Our Great Farmers and Ranchers NEED and DESERVE certainty ahead of the 2027 planting season because FOOD SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY! Congressional Republican Majorities, YOU MUST PASS A NEW FARM BILL DURING THE REMAINING DAYS OF CONGRESS. FARMERS AND RANCHERS ARE NOT INTERESTED IN FURTHER DELAYS,” Trump wrote.

While the House passed its version in April, the Senate has yet to approve its own.

Asked about the upcoming deadlines and GOP priorities on the table, Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) said, “I’m not confident we’re going to do anything.”

Rep. Tony Wied (R-Wis.) said that he’s “not sure” whether Republicans will be able to advance all of their items on the agenda and meet pressing deadlines.

“We have attendance issues, so, I think on both sides, and so at this point I don’t know. I think it’d be a good idea to, and try to get some of these things done, but at this point, I’m not sure,” Wied said.

Some Republicans have been pressing their colleagues to prioritize attendance and ensure the party makes the most of its dwindling time in the majority.

“There is no excuse for not showing up,” Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) said. “They ought to publish every name of everybody and every vote they don’t take. Secondly, we’re at a critical time in this country, and we ought to be up here every day.”

Rep. Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.) said “there’s a lot of things that are very urgent.”

“Certainly the CR, it’s expiring, but there’s a lot of, I would classify, must-pass bills that people recognize,” Newhouse said. “So I’m hopeful that we can come together and do that. You know, I’m a very optimistic person. Being a farmer, you have to be. And I bring that same attitude here. Not naive to the fact that there’s a lot of challenges. People have to show up, and we’ve got some absences. Well, that’s a problem. But we’ve got — I think we’re up to the task, and we’ll get the work done.”

articles.title: Senate Democrats clash over filibuster as progressives eye big agenda
articles.summary: Senate Democrats are clashing over the Senate filibuster, as progressives seek ways to move big, bold reforms next year while more centrist Democrats are warning that could lead to disaster. Several progressives say that when Democrats take control of the Senate next year they should force Republicans to hold the chamber floor with days of…
articles.body:
Senate Democrats are clashing over the Senate filibuster, as progressives seek ways to move big, bold reforms next year while more centrist Democrats are warning that could lead to disaster.

Several progressives say that when Democrats take control of the Senate next year they should force Republicans to hold the chamber floor with days of continuous debate — something known as the talking filibuster — if they try to block Democratic priorities.

As soon as Republican stamina fades and GOP lawmakers stop talking on the floor, Democrats would be able to pass priorities, such as legislation to revive expanded health insurance premium subsidies, with 51 votes. The filibuster requires 60 votes to pass most legislation.

“What I’ve argued for is reforming the filibuster so that if you’re going to have a minority that says they want more debate, they actually have to debate. That debate has to be sustained day and night through the weekend, through the recess,” said Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), a leading proponent of scrapping the filibuster in its current form.

“The current version is an incentive for paralysis. It’s simply a silent tool that doesn’t even include more debate,” he said.

Democrats will control 56 seats in the Senate next year.

Other Senate Democrats are rallying to end the filibuster in its current form.

“I am [a] supporter of the Merkley proposal to restore the filibuster to what it was from the start of the Senate to 1995. I very much support that — the talking filibuster,” Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) said.

“I think it serves a purpose if you do it the way it was originally used,” he said.

That means requiring members of the minority party, who would be Republicans over the next two years, to actively hold the floor by speaking for hours, days or even weeks to stop legislation on the floor.

Centrist Democrats are pushing back on calls to change the rules to allow major bills to pass with 51 votes — warning that they could regret it when Republicans win back control of the Senate.

“I think it would be a mistake, and we just learned over the last two years why,” said Sen. Angus King (Maine), an Independent who caucuses with Democrats. He was referring to Republican proposals that Senate Democrats were able to block since President Trump retook office in January last year.

Democrats were able to defeat Trump’s top priority, the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, which would have required people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote and voters to show photo identification, among other reforms.

Democratic critics of the proposal said the bill could have allowed the Trump administration to disenfranchise millions of Americans.

“Carl Levin once told me, ‘Today’s obnoxious obstructionist, tomorrow’s priceless shield,’” King said, referring to former Sen. Carl Levin’s (D-Mich.) advice that the 60-vote hurdle for passing legislation is essential to preserving the rights of the minority.

The arguments among Senate Democrats over what to do about the filibuster have grown sharper because of Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) insurgent bid to topple Sen. Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) as Senate Democratic leader.

Van Hollen is making it clear in his bid to succeed Schumer that he personally favors getting rid of the Senate’s 60-vote threshold for passing legislation.

“My personal view has been that the filibuster is anti-democratic because you can only end a filibuster — currently you need 60 votes — so that allows 41 senators to block the will of the majority. So yes, I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” he said.

But Van Hollen says “how and when” the filibuster is changed needs to be discussed by the broader Democratic caucus.

He has tried not to alienate Democrats who favor preserving the filibuster by promising that he would not “impose” his view on the caucus.

Van Hollen told The Hill on Friday, “We should begin the conversation early about what kind of obstruction would lead us to consider as a caucus reforming the filibuster.”

“My point is we’ve not had a caucus discussion on the filibuster, and I think it’s an important conversation because there are a lot of things that candidates promised to deliver, especially when it comes to going after political corruption, that will be difficult to deliver without some reform,” he said.

Schumer has largely sidestepped questions in the past about whether he would support overhauling the Senate’s filibuster rule to allow legislation to pass with simple-majority support, though he has favored creating exceptions for what the filibuster applies to, such as voting reform and abortion-rights legislation.

Schumer declined to answer a question immediately after Election Day about whether he would support overhauling the Senate filibuster.

He said in September 2024 that Democrats would discuss creating a “carve-out” in the filibuster rule to pass abortion-rights legislation if they kept the Senate majority in 2025. They wound up losing control of the upper chamber that year, making it a moot issue.

Earlier this year, a group of conservative Republicans led by Sen. Mike Lee (Utah) called on Senate GOP leaders to reinterpret the Senate’s filibuster rule to require continuous debate to stop legislation as part of an effort to pass the SAVE America Act.

“The talking filibuster is the filibuster. I think that is the proper way of understanding what the filibuster is. It’s supposed to involve speaking,” he told The Hill.

Lee says reforming the filibuster rule wouldn’t necessarily require a vote of the Senate.

“You don’t vote for it. It’s a matter of floor management,” he said.

Sen. Mark Warner (Va.) is one of several Democratic centrists warning their liberal colleagues that eliminating the filibuster in its current form would be a big mistake.

“The filibuster saved our country’s bacon over the last couple years a number of times,” Warner told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” in an interview. “I don’t think we ought to get rid of the filibuster.”

Warner told The Hill that the SAVE America Act would have become law without the 60-vote requirement to end a filibuster.

“I still think it’s critically important,” he said of the 60-vote hurdle for passing legislation. “The House will operate under different rules, but the Senate’s always supposed to be the place to temper House legislation.”

But progressives, who are tired of repeated failures to pass bills with majority support through the Senate, say it’s time to change the rules.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), a leading progressive voice, said he likes what Merkley is proposing though he declined to discuss it in detail.

“I think Sen. Merkley has some pretty good ideas,” he said referring to the call for a “talking filibuster” among other proposals.

A Senate Democratic aide said Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) in private meetings has signaled support for getting rid of the 60-vote threshold for passing bills after Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The reason for doing so is that it would allow Democrats to circumvent Republican opposition in the Senate to get popular bills, such as proposals to restore generous subsidies under the Affordable Care Act and reversing cuts to Medicaid, to Trump’s desk.

Warren declined to speak to reporters in the Capitol this past week.

Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), another leading progressive, told Fox News Digital that “the filibuster is something that has to be on the table.”

articles.title: Democrats put campus gambling in the crosshairs
articles.summary: Online sportsbooks and prediction markets are expected to enter a new era of scrutiny from Democrats holding House and Senate majorities in January, with college campuses representing a potential ground zero. As betting platforms grow in popularity and profitability, critics — including some Democrats on Capitol Hill — see U.S. colleges and universities as the…
articles.body:
Online sportsbooks and prediction markets are expected to enter a new era of scrutiny from Democrats holding House and Senate majorities in January, with college campuses representing a potential ground zero.

As betting platforms grow in popularity and profitability, critics — including some Democrats on Capitol Hill — see U.S. colleges and universities as the epicenter of growing gambling addiction issues across the country. They see school officials as being responsible for preventing habitual wagering among students.

“This is a public health crisis unfolding on campuses across America. If we’re serious about protecting students, we have to be honest about how we got here,” said Rep. Alma Adams (D-N.C.), the ranking member on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. “These are predatory products aimed at young people shielded by state law and overseen by a regulatory [body] that’s asleep at the wheel.”

The concern with the speedy growth of gambling in the U.S. stretches across party lines and has intensified with the emergence of prediction markets as an alternative to traditional sportsbooks.

Lawmakers in both parties say they’d like to see prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket regulated the same way major online sportsbooks like DraftKings and FanDuel are at the state level.

The concern comes as industry experts say young people attending universities and colleges in the handful of states where online sports gambling is illegal are especially susceptible to addiction issues in connection with prediction markets.

“Sports prediction markets are sports betting disguised as financial trading,” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) wrote in a social media post this week. “They flout state and tribal gambling laws, siphon state tax revenues, fuel addiction, and expose young Americans to public health risks while evading state consumer safeguards. Congress must ban them.”

Critics of the online gambling industry say most prediction markets have insufficient integrity monitoring processes and weak guardrails against habitual use.

Legal online sportsbooks, many of the same lawmakers say, have relied on aggressive advertising campaigns to market themselves to young people and use enticing promotions targeting habitual users to feed a growing vice.

“It’s clear there’s way too much gambling going on in this country, the question is what can we legally do to stop it,” Rep. Glenn Grothman (R-Wis.), another member of the Education and Workforce Committee. “Particularly at a time when young people don’t have money for a down payment on a house, the idea that they’re spending money on sports betting is kind of ridiculous.”

As is the case with online sportsbooks, studies have shown men younger than 35 years are more likely than any other demographic to use prediction market platforms and experience addiction issues related to excessive wagering.

During a recent hearing, a panel of experts told the House Education and Workforce Committee more students than ever are using financial aid money to wager on sports and current event “contracts.”

Addressing public health concerns related to gambling, and among young people specifically, is a key aim of the Supporting Affordability and Fairness with Every (SAFE) Bet Act, the most significant piece of legislation proposed by Congress on gambling in the past year.

The bill, introduced by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) in the Senate and Rep. Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.) in the House, would set a minimum federal standard to curb predatory practices in the online sports betting industry and implement safeguards for consumers.

But the proposal has gained little traction in the Senate and House under GOP control.

Millions of dollars have poured into lobbying by prediction market platforms and sportsbooks pose a “huge problem” stopping efforts to get legislation like the SAFE Bet Act to a floor vote in either chamber, one lawmaker told The Hill.

“I’m very hopeful it will have some legs in the new Congress because the problems are mounting, and there has to be a much stronger effort to stop gambling among people who are most vulnerable,” Blumenthal said during an interview this week. “Focusing on some [college students] may make sense, but the problem really affects people across the board.”

Some lawmakers have said they would like to see the NCAA do more to work with major colleges and universities to ensure students do not develop gambling problems.

Several members said they were disappointed to see the Protect College Sports Act — a sweeping bill passed by the Senate this year that set regulations on issues like name, image and likeness compensation and the transfer portal — included virtually no language pertaining to sports gambling and athlete harassment.

“We are entering a new frontier with sports betting, I mean … it’s getting into the hands of teenagers,” Rep. Jimmy Patronis (R-Fla.) said. “We’ve not yet passed the college sports bill, and when it comes to amateur sports, you have to have a code of ethics and a death penalty if you get caught with anything related to gambling. If Congress has to get involved, I’m fine with that.”

Republicans like Patronis are telegraphing a willingness to work with Democrats to address gambling’s potentially harmful growth on college campuses once the GOP cedes control of both chambers come the new year.

“We need to see plans from universities on how they’re going to look at problematic gaming and build an expectation that they are educating their students about substance abuse like they do alcohol, drugs and sexual assault,” said Rep. Michael Baumgartner (R-Wash.), who led the recent House hearing examining gambling on college campuses.

“After the election cycle and everything being so partisan around here, I thought that hearing was really cathartic in the sense like this is what Congress is actually supposed to be doing.”

Don’t ask Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira (R-Texas) about the Congressional Baseball Game next spring because he’s done talking about it. The former New York Yankees slugger was on Capitol Hill this week for new member orientation and got short with Fox News host Stuart Varney when the anchor asked him about his excitement level ahead of the annual charity baseball game pitting Republicans against Democrats. “I’m sure we will win again, but quite frankly, I’m tired of talking about this game,” Teixeira said. “I didn’t come here to play baseball. I came here to deliver for the American people.”

It has been a bizarre few days at East Potomac Golf Links, where the public park remains open because of a federal judge’s order but no operator for the golf courses is present. Golfers continued to show up at East Potomac last week despite a lack of flag sticks, tee markers and grass growing increasingly long on the Hains Point property. Judge Ana Reyes is expected to rule in the coming weeks on President Trump’s bid to take over and redevelop the property, while the Justice Department says it will appeal her recent ruling halting further work by the administration there.

President Trump awarded a posthumous pardon to legendary MLB player Pete Rose on Thursday. In a Truth Social post, the president said Rose had been “treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame.” Rose was infamously banned from MLB for life for betting on baseball and later served five months in federal prison for tax evasion. He was later reinstated by MLB after lobbying from Trump and died in 2024.

Jocks on the Hill: Rep. Scott Fitzgerald (R-Wis.)

Rep. Scott Fitzgerald (R-Wis.), a former local newspaper publisher in Wisconsin, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“I love football, both playing in high school and watching now. I love it.”

“Green Bay Packers. They looked great the other night!”

Is there an athlete you really admired growing up?

“The guy that I always followed and was interesting to watch was Michael Jordan because he was such an international celebrity and dominated for so many years. Nothing original, he has many fans, but it’s definitely Michael Jordan.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you love to root against?

“Well, when you represent Wisconsin in Congress, it’s gotta be the Chicago Bears, although the further to the west you get, it’s the Vikings.”

Sports and politics are both full of cliches, is there one that resonates with you?

“You gotta be good at a sport to be one.”

The Athletic’s Dan Robson has a harrowing profile of former NHL goalie Jack Campbell, who has spoken openly about his struggles with mental health and self-image.

If you can believe it, college basketball is back. And Sports Illustrated examined a growing trend during the regular season: neutral site games that come with high-dollar ticket prices.

Tech giant Anthropic went public last week, which means some of the company’s top employees are set to receive major paydays. Sportico’s Jacob Feldman predicts some of them could be part of the next generation’s sports billionaire class.

articles.title: Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court
articles.summary: Brian Morales García of Texas seeks damages after he was wrongly identified as undocumented in case White House wants dropped
articles.body:
The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.

Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.

Morales García's case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress .

The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.

Morales García was his boss's passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn't believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.

Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.

Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.

Morales García's attorneys sued on 1 May, maintaining that he had falsely said he entered the US illegally and signed papers for a rapid deportation in response to threats of imprisonment by agents. His lawsuit, which seeks an unspecified amount of money, also contended that family and friends tried to deliver documents proving his US citizenship before this deportation.

But those efforts were unduly rebuffed, Morales García's lawsuit said.

The Trump administration denied Morales García's assertions, saying on Friday that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore lacked any basis to sue the federal government for damages. Nonetheless, in court filings on Friday, the administration conceded that Morales García "was permitted entry" back into the US on 30 August after it reviewed "information concerning plaintiff's place of birth".

"Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico," Justin Simmons, the US attorney for the western district of Texas, wrote in a court filing first reported by the Texas Tribune .

Americans are not required to carry proof of citizenship when going about their daily business. Lawyers across the US have seen cases such as Morales García's, which begin after an encounter with local authorities demonstrate how those officials are generally not aware of the nuances of immigration policy.

Texas's public safety department is among many US state and local agencies that collaborate with federal immigration authorities under their 287(g) program .

The judge presiding over Morales García's lawsuit, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the Trump administration's request on Friday to dismiss the case. The lawsuit also named unspecified local and state Texas law enforcement officers as defendants.

An October 2025 report by ProPublica found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump's second presidency.

Meanwhile, the media statement incorrectly saying Morales García was in the US illegally is among several related to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration that has unraveled under scrutiny.

A Guardian analysis published in July reviewed Trump administration press releases on 26 cases of cars allegedly being used to assault immigration enforcement agents – and nearly all were either disproven or dropped.

articles.title: Trump to confront Newsom over plan to spare 548 death row inmates, including notorious child killers
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is expected to join victims' families at the DOJ to condemn Gavin Newsom's plan to commute all 548 California death sentences to life without parole.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — President Donald Trump will confront California Gov. Gavin Newsom over his sweeping plan to spare 548 death row inmates from execution, including a man who murdered nine members of his own family, the killer of 12-year-old Polly Klaas and the man convicted of torturing 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez to death. Trump is expected to appear alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel at the Department of Justice (DOJ) on Monday afternoon to condemn the Democratic governor's proposed commutations, the White House confirmed to Fox News Digital. Families of murder victims are expected to attend the event, where their stories will be highlighted as the Trump administration challenges Newsom's effort to replace every California death sentence with life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. NEWSOM'S BID TO EMPTY CALIFORNIA'S DEATH ROW COLLIDES WITH VOTERS' REPEATED REJECTION OF ABOLITION "Governor Newsom is failing the victims and their families by refusing to carry out justice against these barbaric child killers and serial killers. These murderers raped, tortured and terrorized innocent victims. Governor Newsom must stop playing politics with public safety," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intended to commute all 548 California death sentences to life imprisonment without parole, arguing that capital punishment is incompatible with the state's values. Asked by Fox News Digital about the proposed commutations, Newsom's office did not directly address the individual murder cases highlighted by the White House. Instead, the governor's office referred Fox News Digital to his previously published letter defending the decision. "California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books, and I respect that," Newsom wrote. "But the constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice. For me, this is that moment." Newsom also acknowledged that some victims' families strongly oppose his decision, while his office pointed to other survivors who support eliminating capital punishment. The White House provided Fox News Digital with a list of 20 notorious convicted killers who would benefit from Newsom's proposed clemency, detailing crimes involving murdered children, sexual violence, torture and serial killings. NEWSOM ORDERS CALIFORNIA’S MOST REVILED KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW – 10 OF THE WORST WHO COULD BENEFIT Among them is Marcus Wesson, who was convicted of murdering nine members of his family in Fresno, including children and grandchildren. Wesson was also convicted of rape and sexual abuse involving his daughters and nieces, whom he subjected to years of abuse within a cult-like family structure. Richard Allen Davis was sentenced to death for kidnapping and murdering 12-year-old Polly Klaas, who was abducted from a sleepover at her Petaluma home in 1993. The case shocked the nation and helped galvanize support for California's three-strikes sentencing law. The White House also highlighted Isauro Aguirre, convicted of the torture and murder of 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez in Los Angeles County. Gabriel suffered prolonged abuse before his death, a case that drew national outrage and later became the subject of a documentary series examining the violence he endured and failures to protect him. Other offenders identified by the White House include Charles Ng, convicted of 11 murders involving captivity, torture and sexual violence, and Randy Kraft, the so-called "Scorecard Killer," convicted of murdering 16 men in crimes involving sexual assault and mutilation. Chester Turner, convicted of murdering 14 women in Los Angeles, and Cary Stayner, convicted of four murders near Yosemite National Park, were also named. Some of the cases involved the slaughter of entire families. Ramon Salcido was convicted of killing seven people during a Sonoma County rampage, including his wife and two young daughters, while former school administrator Vincent Brothers was convicted of murdering his wife, three children and mother-in-law in Bakersfield. The White House's intervention comes as Newsom faces mounting opposition from California prosecutors and victims' advocates who argue that his sweeping clemency plan disregards the verdicts of juries and the suffering of families who spent years pursuing justice. CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART' Although the condemned inmates would remain behind bars for life without the possibility of parole, the commutations would permanently remove the prospect of execution, regardless of the wishes of families who continue to seek that outcome. "I was just sickened, frankly, for the crime victims in California who were slapped in the face by our governor," San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow previously told Fox News Digital. Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer previously accused Newsom of extending "mercy for the wolves … while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep." The proposed commutations have not yet taken effect. Under California law, 382 requires a recommendation from the state Supreme Court because the inmates have multiple felony convictions. Newsom's administration has said it will not proceed with any of the commutations until the court acts. The legal battle intensified last week when a coalition of California prosecutors and victims' advocates asked the state Supreme Court to halt the plan, arguing that Newsom failed to provide victims and their families an opportunity to be heard before pursuing the sweeping clemency action. The court has invited additional briefs through Tuesday, Nov. 24, as it considers the governor's request. Newsom has asked the justices to act before his term ends in January. California voters rejected efforts to abolish the death penalty in 2012 and 2016. The state has not carried out an execution since 2006, and Newsom imposed a formal moratorium on capital punishment shortly after taking office in 2019. Trump has taken the opposite approach, directing the Justice Department on his first day back in office to prioritize seeking and implementing lawful death sentences. In April, the department announced additional measures to strengthen federal capital punishment procedures, including reinstating its previous lethal injection protocol and expanding available execution methods. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APPRepresentatives from the FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration, U.S. Marshals Service, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Federal Bureau of Prisons are also expected to attend Monday's event.Fox News Digital's Louis Casiano contributed to this reporting.

articles.title: DNC debate plan demands ‘dark money’ pledge
articles.summary: The plan announced Monday morning includes 12 debates, but only if candidates make the pledge.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) —The Democratic National Committee will hold 12 presidential primary debates and any candidate who wants to participate must sign a pledge denouncing dark money, according to the framework the DNC announced Monday morning.

While the number of debates and the requirements appear similar to the 2020 Democratic primary, the dark money pledge is new, as is the explicit incorporation of digital creators and influencers in the debates.

The DNC plans to hold five debates in 2027 with the first two taking place in June and July. The final seven will take place in 2028, with six of them held in early-primary states. The final debate is scheduled to take place in March 2028. Further details, including specific dates and locations will start to be announced this coming January.

The DNC expects a crowded field of candidates and therefore says they will need to cap debates at 20 candidates. If necessary, debates will be split into two consecutive nights as was done in the 2020 primary, and the DNC will ensure that any candidates deemed frontrunners are split between the two nights.

To qualify, candidates will need to meet certain criteria including polling and other measures that indicate the support a candidate has from the electorate. The DNC offered grassroots fundraising as an example, but all specific details are still forthcoming.

Creators and influencers will be incorporated into the debate process in an effort to maximize viewership.

Called the Fair Campaign Practices Pledge, candidates will have to denounce dark money spending in an effort to limit its influence and that of special interests.

The DNC says the pledge is meant to cover outside groups like political nonprofits or super PACs that do not disclose their donors and don’t adhere to federal contribution limits.

Spending by entities that violate the pledge requires the candidate to denounce said spending in order to participate in future debates.

The DNC’s website says , “In the wake of the Citizens United Supreme Court decision, dark money and independent spending have exploded, increasing the influence of special interests in politics.” Since the DNC does not have legal authority to ban super PACs or dark money groups, they have created this pledge.

The website says the full reporting process will be available, including a tracker with all the submitted complaints, their adjudication status, and denunciations.

This pledge does not impact the general election. The DNC says their goal is to get dark money out of the primary process.

A DNC official said the pledge has so far received the support of Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Andy Kim, D-N.J., as well as Reps. Greg Casar, D-Texas, and Jason Crow, D-Colo., along with former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison.

“The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we’re announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee, and put Democrats in position to take back the White House,” says DNC chair Ken Martin.

The leadership team includes DNC Senior Advisor for Debates Minyon Moore and DNC Executive Director Roger Lau. The Debate Planning Committee writ large includes former advisors and staff from the 2020 presidential campaigns of President Joe Biden and Senators Sanders, Warren, and Amy Klobuchar, plus others who worked on the campaigns of Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Kamala Harris.

While no one has officially declared candidacy yet, allies of several potential candidates launched committees to encourage them to run. They include Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Ro Khanna, D-Calif., as well as former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

The Republican National Committee has not released their primary debate schedule.

articles.title: GOP senator 'not likely' to mount presidential bid, but continues leaving door open to possibility
articles.summary: Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana is continuing to leave the door open to the possibility of mounting a 2028 bid for the presidency.
articles.body: Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., is continuing to leave the door open to the possibility of mounting a 2028 presidential bid, though he said that such a move is "not likely" and that he plans to seek re-election. "My plan right now is to run for re-election," Kennedy told Kristen Welker during an interview that aired on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday. "If I get fed up with things and catch a wild hair and have a, I don't know, a spontaneous moment of ... questionable genius, if I get really fed up I could run. But it's not likely," he said, noting that he plans to pursue re-election. DEMOCRATS SIZE UP 2028 IN DENVER. WE ASKED WHO'S READY TO RUN Kennedy has served in the Senate since early 2017. His current term ends in early 2029, so if he wants to seek a third Senate term, he will need to run in 2028. President Donald Trump, who is currently serving his second term, is constitutionally barred from being elected president again. REPUBLICAN SENATOR OPENS DOOR ON POSSIBILITY OF A PRESIDENTIAL BID, IN SHIFT FROM PAST POSITION During a "Meet the Press" interview that aired last month, Kennedy also told Welker that he planned to seek re-election. "But as I've said before," he told Welker last month regarding the idea of a presidential run, "if I don't think I can be effective in the Senate anymore I would consider it." NEWSOM REVEALS WHEN HE'LL DECIDE ON 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID AMID GROWING SPECULATION CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He said during that appearance in October that if a group of "goobers" runs on his side of the aisle, "and I think I could do a better job, I would consider runnin'. But right now I'm runnin' for re-election."

articles.title: Democrats reveal aggressive debate plan for 2028 presidential race
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Dems setting the stage for 2028 ▪ Army preparing Iowa detonation ▪ Largest House majority this century clinched ▪ COP31 ends without agreement The Democratic National Committee (DNC) released its presidential debate schedule Monday morning as the party seeks to build off its sweeping midterm victories and take back the White…
articles.body:
▪ Largest House majority this century clinched

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) released its presidential debate schedule Monday morning as the party seeks to build off its sweeping midterm victories and take back the White House.

The DNC plans to hold 12 debates throughout the presidential cycle, with five in 2027 and seven in 2028. The first ones will be held in June and July, with specific dates, locations, media partners and other details to be announced in January.

This is the earliest that the DNC has ever announced its debate framework ahead of a presidential cycle, the party said, reflecting their eagerness to win the presidency back after a crushing defeat in 2024 that brought President Trump back to power.

The Democratic shadow primary is already well underway, as rumored contenders make moves publicly and privately to set themselves up for a run.

Vice President Kamala Harris has been openly weighing another bid after her abbreviated 2024 run that fell short. Some of her backers launched a Run, Kamala, Run PAC earlier this month to support her candidacy should she get in the race.

Harris has led other potential Democrats in various hypothetical 2028 polls, but she’s far from the only one who has been flirting with a bid.

Progressives organized their own group called Ready for AOC earlier this month to build a grassroots infrastructure if Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) decides to run for the Oval Office.

Ocasio-Cortez has been mulling what her next move should be. She’s expressed interest in both running for the presidency or Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer ‘s (D) Senate seat in New York. She’s said she would decide after the midterms and recently overhauled her team for the second time in the past few months.

If Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t run for president, progressive enthusiasm may turn to Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). Just two days after the midterms, his supporters launched an effort to draft the congressman into the race.

Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg , who has also led some early polls, launched a new fundraising committee on Thursday to urge the former 2020 contender to make another try.

Team Pete PAC isn’t directly associated with Buttigieg himself, but the former South Bend, Ind., mayor has made several recent moves that have fueled speculation he’ll try again. Buttigieg was a vigorous advocate on the campaign trail for Democrats during the midterms, and he has a book set to come out in January.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) has made no secret that he’s considering a run, but he has placed a condition that he wouldn’t run if Harris does so , saying in September that they would be fighting over similar bases.

A few of the big winners of the midterms have also been the subject of 2028 speculation both before and after Election Day.

Both Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) pulled off overwhelming reelection victories in key battleground states. Shapiro hasn’t directly addressed the possibility of his own presidential bid, while Ossoff has maintained that he isn’t interested. That hasn’t quelled the speculation though.

Other rumored possible Democratic contenders include Maryland Gov. Wes Moore , Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Sen. Mark Kelly (Ariz.).

One aspect of the coming race that many analysts seem to agree on is a wide field that could at least approach a record number of candidates.

The DNC included plans for a potentially large field. Early debates may take place over two nights, with the total number of candidates participating capped at 20. The lineups for each night will be decided at random to ensure parity across both nights.

That arrangement would avoid the so-called undercard debates that featured the candidates not performing as well in the polls during the 2020 cycle.

The DNC will lay out certain criteria to determine who will qualify for the debates, including polling and other objective measures such as grassroots fundraising. Candidates will also need to abide by the DNC’s rules to ensure a fair process, including signing a fair campaign practices pledge to denounce dark money spending.

“Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” said DNC Chair Ken Martin . “The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we’re announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee, and put Democrats in position to take back the White House.”

▪ The Hill : Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) leaves door open for 2028 run.

▪ The Hill : Dems want ‘Medicare for More.’ Then comes the hard part.

Delta Air Lines said its automated system that calculates an aircraft’s weight is working once again after an issue disrupted the system for hours on Sunday. Staff used manual workarounds to get flights going in the meantime, but more than 2,000 Delta flights were delayed as a result of the error.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) has released 84,000 more records related to the impacts that the 9/11 attacks had on the air quality of the city, the third installment of records being made public. Past releases suggested how city leaders misled the public about dangerous toxins in the air.

Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the scandal that toppled former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, was in touch with China’s spy agency during their affair, according to The New York Times . Trump was told twice about the links, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the briefings.

This photo provided by the U.S. Army shows the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on May 14, 2024. (Shawn Eldridge/U.S. Army via AP)

WON’T STOP : The Army is pressing ahead with its plans for a detonation of more than 60 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant despite legal blocks and significant objections from locals concerned about the impact on public safety.

Lawyers for the Justice Department argued the controlled detonation is necessary to protect the public from the “more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion.” The Army said Sunday night the detonation had been pushed back to Wednesday “to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.”

A federal court halted the detonation on Friday as environmental groups argued it could expose thousands of families in the surrounding communities to toxic dust. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit paused the explosions indefinitely, but the Justice Department is arguing that it doesn’t need to follow the blocks because of public safety risks that the barrels pose if left undetonated.

“Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay,” the lawyers said.

Both federal and state lawmakers across the political aisle have expressed concern about the Trump administration’s plans. Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) said the administration has provided an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity.”

Rep. Ashley Hinson (R), who was defeated in a race for Iowa’s Senate seat this month, said the surrounding communities weren’t given “adequate notice” and called for the detonation to be delayed until the impact on local air quality could be studied.

▪ The New York Times : Army rejected cleaner option to destroy barrels.

HIGH WATER MARK : Democrats have officially secured the largest House majority in more than three decades as they clinched at least 258 seats on Sunday.

Decision Desk HQ projected that Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) hours after a recount confirmed Hubbard’s lead and Foxx conceded defeat. Hubbard won by just more than 330 votes, pulling off a major flip in North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District, viewed as a safe Republican district.

Foxx, the chair of the House Rules Committee, is the final domino to fall in North Carolina as Republicans’ redistricting efforts backfired. Instead of picking up one additional seat, the GOP lost seven of its own seats in what became the country’s most resounding “dummymander.”

The race call officially secures a larger House majority for Democrats than they had even at the start of former President Obama ‘s term. The last time they won this many was in 1992, and the party is hoping to pick up a couple more with the few remaining uncalled races.

The Hill’s Julia Mueller breaks down for Insiders the outstanding House races that will decide how many seats will make up the Democrats’ final majority.

▪ The Hill Insider : How Democrats plan to bring prices down.

‘HARD QUESTIONS’ : Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said he wants to hear more from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick about how he’s working to prevent China from accessing U.S. chips in the aftermath of the Nvidia scandal.

Kennedy said during an appearance on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that the Commerce Department “appears” to have allowed China to get around export controls to get access to advanced chips. Lutnick has faced scrutiny following Jensen Huang ‘s resignation amid reports that he’s taken a soft stance on the export controls.

“Let’s answer some hard questions,” Kennedy said. “And if Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion.”

▪ The Hill : Tom Cotton claims Lutnick ignored warning letters.

▪ The Wall Street Journal : Lutnick is the ultimate survivor in the administration.

The president will receive an intelligence briefing at 11 a.m. He will deliver remarks on protecting American families at the Department of Justice at 4:30 p.m.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) speaks to reporters after the House Democratic Caucus chose him as their nominee to be Speaker in the 120th Congress, at the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 18, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite)

HOUSE DIVIDED : House Democrats are split on their strategy toward the Iran war during the lame-duck session.

Some in the party want to demand an end to funding for the war, which could result in a shutdown next month, while others want to punt the battle until next year, when Democrats will take control of both houses of Congress.

The Hill’s Mike Lillis reports that liberals are feeling emboldened by the midterm results and want to use Democrats’ leverage are on one side, while other top Democrats oppose the war but aren’t ready to shut down the government over it.

“We’re going to fight to get that Iran funding removed for offensive military capability,” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), a key progressive.

“I frankly want to … end the funding to the Iran war. But shutting the government down doesn’t stop the war,” said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (Conn.), the senior Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee.

The internal battle has also been taking place in the Senate, with the debate growing sharper as Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) challenges Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for majority leader.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), who is in line to become chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and has been involved in government funding negotiations, suggested to Lillis that Democrats are searching for ways to restrict Trump’s military operations in Iran without a complete defunding, which Republicans would likely oppose and potentially lead to a shutdown.

“So we’ve got to figure it out,” he said.

Sens. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), members of the Senate Armed Services Committee, announced on Thursday that they will move to add an amendment to appropriations bills to block funding for offensive operations against Iran.

▪ The Hill : Hakeem Jeffries faces growing pains with large majority, sprawling agenda.

▪ The Hill Insider : This Week: Lawmakers break for Thanksgiving.

People attend a closing plenary session at the COP31 United Nations Climate Summit on Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. (AP Photo/Khalil Hamra)

COP OUT : The United Nations’s annual climate conference failed to reach a consensus between governments around the world over a clash concerning fossil fuel regulation.

COP31 was extended two additional days into the weekend after almost two weeks of talks to try to give more time for negotiations, but a consensus was still not reached. This is the third time in the climate summit’s three-decade history that negotiators failed to reach an agreement.

The first one was at COP6 in 2000, and the second one was at COP15 in 2009.

The participants butted heads as top oil-producing countries like Russia and Saudi Arabia blocked mentions of phasing out fossil fuels while the European Union rejected proposals that would have cut certain protections and favored countries that export oil, gas and coal.

The Associated Press reported that another source of conflict was whether ramping up electricity should only be done with renewable resources or involve energy sources like natural gas.

“The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now,” U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement. “The countries that did least to cause this crisis cannot be left to face its worst consequences alone. This is a matter of climate justice.”

The Trump administration didn’t directly participate in the conference. The U.S. is one of the largest polluters in the world.

▪ The Hill : Trump hates wind power, but a bill he supports may help it.

▪ The Hill : Meta reevaluating net zero goal amid AI boom.

Impeaching Hegseth is a trap Democrats should avoid , David Wippman and Glenn C. Altschuler writes in The Hill.

This Thanksgiving , be grateful for James Madison , Chris Taux writes in The Hill.

Clouds roll behind the Washington Monument on the National Mall on Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Allison Robbert)

And finally … A group of at least a couple dozen people gathered Sunday in the nation’s capital for the seemingly impossible task of moving the Washington Monument.

A Partiful invite, which hundreds of people RSVP’d yes to, called on people to come together to push the monument a few inches to the left to better align it with the White House. A video from Axios reporter Andrew Solender shows the handful of people pushing either with their hands or their backs to try to move the monument.

The push may have drawn some inspiration from a crowd that gathered to move The Bean in Chicago’s Millennium Park earlier this month, with a similar result.

articles.title: A new week, a few new black eyes for national political journalism
articles.summary: Are the media determined to get back into the running for America’s least-trusted institution?
articles.body:
For an industry that considers itself the last line of defense against the cancer of misinformation, last week wasn’t corporate media’s best showing. From failing the basics of investigative journalism to bungling basic legalese, the press’s slowly but surely recovering reputation took a couple of solid hits.

Two ABC News staffers may be on the chopping block following the publication of a report in early October that claimed firms closely linked to President Trump’s sons, Eric and Donald Jr., had been awarded more than $6 billion in defense contracts. The initial reporting was simply false, with nearly every major claim either incorrect or overstated. But now we learn that the two ABC journalists responsible for the story are on paid leave, according to the New York Post .

That makes sense. The story was a mess. After it ran in early October, ABC retracted it almost immediately with no notice or warning. Then, after more than 24 hours of silence, the story resurfaced with a major facelift, republished under a completely new headline, with a completely new framing. The $6 billion figure was removed, as was the name of the original author. The byline for the reworked version, which is still live, simply reads “ABC News.”

At the time, sources at ABC claimed the story had simply been published prematurely , an excuse whose believability was stretched thin by both the network’s odd handling of the issue and the sheer volume of rewrites. Now, an internal ABC investigation has allegedly discovered that, among many other flaws in the initial reporting, the story’s authors never even reached out for comment to one of the firms at the center of the report. That’s one way to get a story so badly wrong.

Speaking of badly overstating things, there was also The New York Times, which managed last week to fail even worse than ABC, precisely because the paper cannot even hide behind the flimsy excuse that it failed to reach out for comment.

On Nov. 10, the Times reported that the past two decades’ worth of Second Amendment legal precedent has hinged entirely on a misquotation made by the late Justice Antonin Scalia. The story reads like a conspiracy theory and sounds like something a Sovereign Citizen might say in court to deny the legitimacy of its proceedings.

In his opinion for the 2008 Heller case, Scalia argued that legal tradition supports only the prohibition of “dangerous and unusual weapons,” he thereafter cited numerous legal sources, including the jurist William Blackstone, whose treatises on common law laid the foundation of U.S. law, including the Second Amendment.

The Times’ quibble is that Blackstone actually wrote, “dangerous or unusual,” not “dangerous and unusual” — a tiny but pivotal difference, or so the newspaper contended. But the quibble is misplaced, because Scalia wasn’t misquoting anyone. A look at the Supreme Court’s style guide would have made that clear.

In his opinion, Scalia’s reference to Blackstone came only after his use of a “see” signal. In other words, Scalia was pointing readers to a list of legal sources using similar language, just one of which was Blackstone. And Blackstone did use “or,” but Scalia was also pointing to multiple other legal sources that had used “and” between the descriptors “dangerous” and “unusual.” The Supreme Court’s style guide notes that the “see” signal is not for direct quotations, but rather to indicate that “the cited authority is basic source material supporting, although not stating, the text proposition.”

Thus, “Blackstone is cited first, not because it is the dominant source, but because the authorities are listed in chronological order,” the Volokh Conspiracy’s Jonathan Adler notes.

It would be one thing had the Times merely bungled the legalese. But the paper also reportedly reached out to John Bash, who clerked for Scalia, and then completely ignored his explanation. Bash said he spoke at length with the Times , correcting their misunderstanding about the legal language of the opinion. He said he gave a “full on-the-record explanation,” clarifying what the paper clearly believed to be a misquotation which, according to the Times’ framing, “judges across the country have invoked … to strike down gun-control laws.”

Nothing Bash said made it into the Times’ final report, nor did any reference to the interview.

The paper maintained last week that its reporting is sound. The Times’ article reported that Justice Scalia wrongly attributed the direct quote “dangerous and unusual” to the jurist William Blackstone, the paper said in a defensive public statement. “That is a fact, and one that has also been recognized by a federal appeals court. This reporting is an accurate portrayal of what Justice Scalia did.” But it isn’t. Protest all they want, but as Adler noted, “It seems to me the Times is still not accounting for the meaning of the ‘see’ signal.”

Lastly, across the Potomac and doing nothing to help media hold on to its recent bump in public confidence, the Washington Post published a news blurb that seemingly blamed former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin (R), a Republican, for the state’s withdrawal from the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program. Its coverage made it seem as if the current governor, Democratic moonbeam Abigail Spanberger (D), is somehow a passive or totally nonexistent player in all of this.

“Exclusive,” declared the blurb, “Despite months of former governor Glenn Youngkin (R) touting his decision to enroll Virginia in a new federal school voucher program, his administration did not complete the process, and his successor will reverse Youngkin’s decision.”

It takes a special kind of talent to see a Democratic governor withdraw from a program for gifted students — even turning down free money in the process — and then turn the story somehow into something about her Republican predecessor. The blurb failed even to mention Spanberger by name, let alone her party affiliation, which was a nice touch.

In the Post’s defense, on its website, behind a paywall, it went with the more accurate headline: “Spanberger reverses Virginia plan to participate in Trump’s school vouchers.”

For better coverage, try the Richmond Times-Dispatch , which announced: “Gov. Abigail Spanberger has pulled Virginia out of the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, a new program starting next January that will provide scholarships available to most K-12 students in participating states.”

Extreme low trust in media has long been a huge problem, so it is heartening to see the modest uptick recently detected by the Pew Research Center’s survey. But there’s no need to put that to the test, unless the media are determined to get back into the running for America’s least-trusted institution.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: 'Failed socialist state': Deep blue state’s lone GOP congressman reveals secret to winning as Democrats sweep
articles.summary: Rep. Cliff Bentz told Fox News Digital that Oregon voters rejected failed progressive policies, blaming high taxes and regulation for hurting business.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Oregon's lone Republican congressman told Fox News Digital that voters in his district rejected what he described as the state's "failed" progressive policies, offering the GOP a roadmap for winning back voters after Democrats' midterm sweep. Rep. Cliff Bentz, R-Ore., who won his fourth term in Congress by over 70,000 votes, with a total of 61% of the vote, made his remarks after securing re-election despite a nationwide Democratic wave that handed Republicans significant losses in Congress and state elections. "My folks wanted someone that they could depend upon when it comes to protecting business and trying to reverse this horrible trend toward more, in this you have a failed state than anything else," Bentz told Fox News Digital. FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM' The congressman argued that his continued electoral success stems from highlighting what he considers the economic consequences of Democratic leadership in Oregon, particularly policies enacted in the state capital. "Crazy, crazy Democrat policies emanating out of Salem, the capital of Oregon," Bentz said, pointing to what he described as "the ridiculous impact of these policies." Bentz blamed high taxes and progressive regulations for hurting businesses and contributing to Oregon's declining quality of life, arguing that voters are increasingly frustrated with the state's political direction. Oregon has a 9.9% state income tax rate, a top corporate income tax of 7.6% and a 0.57% corporate activity tax rate, which he believes has driven the local economy to a near collapse. The state legislature has recently enacted policies such as ones that require certain large employers in retail, hospitality and food service to provide advance work schedules, which critics argue limits scheduling flexibility. REPUBLICANS NEED HISTORY LESSON ABOUT THEIR PARTY IF THEY WANT TO MOVE ON FROM DEFEAT The Republican also suggested that his party could regain ground nationally by adopting a similar approach, particularly as Republicans prepare to enter the minority in Congress. Democrats outnumber Republicans by nearly 100 seats in the House, and 10 seats in the Senate. "When you're in the minority, you can start calling out the stupidity of the opponent's approach to the economy and to regulation," Bentz told Fox News Digital. "So you start out by saying, 'Hey, if you want more of this, well, just keep voting for it,'" he continued. Bentz argued that Republicans should use their time in the minority to highlight the economic consequences of Democratic policies and present themselves as an alternative to progressive governance.
